lead: A flat panel can buckle under in-plane shear alone. Shear is tension along one diagonal and compression along the other, and the compression diagonal wrinkles the plate into inclined waves. Spar webs, fuselage side panels and wing skins between stringers carry shear and compression together, and each load then lowers the load the other can carry. The safe combinations lie inside an interaction curve, and for compression with shear that curve is not a circle.
prereq: You need: Ncr = kπ²D/b² and the critical stress formula from buckling of thin plates.

sections.h3: Shear buckling and the coefficient k<sub>s</sub>

blocks.text: A shear force per unit length N<sub>xy</sub> (N/m) on the edges of a plate gives a shear stress τ = N<sub>xy</sub>/t. On axes at 45° this is equal tension and compression. The compressed diagonal behaves like a strut and can buckle, so the plate wrinkles in waves inclined to the edges. The buckling equation is the same as for compression, with the N<sub>xy</sub> term, and its lowest root has the same form:
N<sub>xy,cr</sub> = k<sub>s</sub> π²D/b²,   τ<sub>cr</sub> = k<sub>s</sub> π²E/[12(1 − ν²)] × (t/b)²
blocks.where: N<sub>xy,cr</sub> is the critical shear force per unit length (N/m); τ<sub>cr</sub> the critical shear stress (Pa); k<sub>s</sub> the shear buckling coefficient; D the plate stiffness (N·m); b the shorter side of the panel (m).

blocks.text: k<sub>s</sub> ≈ 5.35 + 4(b/a)²   (all edges simply supported, a ≥ b)
blocks.where: a is the longer side (m). A square plate has k<sub>s</sub> ≈ 9.35; a long strip tends to 5.35.

blocks.text: Clamped edges raise k<sub>s</sub>; it is read from charts for that case and must not be mixed with the simply supported fit. Because k<sub>s</sub> for shear is larger than k<sub>c</sub> = 4 for compression, a panel takes a larger shear stress than compressive stress before buckling, but webs are thin and their shear buckling stress is still only a few MPa.

When several loads act, express each as a ratio to the stress that would buckle the panel under that load alone: R<sub>c</sub> = σ/σ<sub>cr</sub> for compression and R<sub>s</sub> = τ/τ<sub>cr</sub> for shear. Buckling occurs when the combination reaches an interaction curve. Tests and analysis give curves of the general form R₁ˣ + R₂ʸ = 1, with exponents that depend on the loads and the panel. For a long flat panel under longitudinal compression and shear:

blocks.where: R<sub>c</sub> is the compressive stress ratio σ/σ<sub>cr</sub> and R<sub>s</sub> the shear stress ratio τ/τ<sub>cr</sub>, each with its single-load critical stress.

blocks.text: The shear ratio is squared because shear of either sign is equally bad: reversing the shear only mirrors the inclined buckle, so the curve must be symmetric in R<sub>s</sub>. Compression enters linearly. Inside the curve the panel is unbuckled. The curve lies outside the straight line R<sub>c</sub> + R<sub>s</sub> = 1 but inside the circle R<sub>c</sub>² + R<sub>s</sub>² = 1, so using the circle for this case is unsafe.
If all loads grow in proportion by a factor λ, buckling happens when λR<sub>c</sub> + λ²R<sub>s</sub>² = 1. Solving the quadratic gives the reserve factor and the margin of safety:

blocks.where: λ is the factor on the applied loads at buckling; MS the margin of safety, positive when the panel does not buckle.

blocks.text: Other combinations, such as bending with shear in a spar web, or biaxial compression, have their own interaction curves with different exponents, taken from design charts.

τ<sub>cr</sub> is the onset of buckling, not collapse. A thin web that has buckled in shear keeps carrying load as a diagonal tension field, anchored by its flanges and stiffeners; the analysis is the tension field theory of thin-webbed beams. Many aircraft webs are designed to buckle well below their ultimate load. A skin that must stay smooth for aerodynamics or to support stringers, however, is sized so that the combined ratio stays inside the curve at limit load, and repeated buckling in service needs a fatigue check at the wrinkle crests and the rivets.

figure.caption: The first worked example on the interaction diagram. The applied stresses (R<sub>c</sub> = 0.45, R<sub>s</sub> = 0.52) lie inside the curve R<sub>c</sub> + R<sub>s</sub>² = 1; scaling both by λ = 1.263 reaches it, a margin of 0.26. At 12 MPa compression the curve allows R<sub>s</sub> = 0.741 (28.5 MPa of shear); the circle would allow 0.892 (34.4 MPa), which is unsafe.

spec.aria: A graph of shear ratio R s against compression ratio R c, both from 0 to 1.1. A solid curve R c plus R s squared equals 1 runs from (0, 1) to (1, 0), bulging outward. A dashed quarter circle lies outside it and a dotted straight line inside it. The applied point at 0.45, 0.52 is inside the solid curve, with a dashed ray from the origin through it reaching the curve at a factor of 1.263. Directly above the point, the solid curve is crossed at 0.741 and the circle at 0.892.

examples.question: A wing skin panel between two stringers and two ribs is 600 mm long and 200 mm wide, 2 mm thick, with E = 72 GPa and ν = 0.33 and simply supported edges. It carries a compressive stress of 12 MPa and a shear stress of 20 MPa. Find the two critical stresses, check the panel, find its margin of safety, and find the largest shear it can take with the 12 MPa compression.
steps: Compression: a/b = 3, a whole number, so k<sub>c</sub> = 4 and σ<sub>cr</sub> = 4 × 66,455 × 10⁻⁴ = 26.58 MPa.
Check: R<sub>c</sub> + R<sub>s</sub>² = 0.4514 + 0.2698 = 0.721 < 1, so the panel does not buckle.
Largest shear at 12 MPa compression: R<sub>s</sub> = √(1 − 0.4514) = 0.7407, τ = 0.7407 × 38.51 = 28.5 MPa.
The circle R<sub>c</sub>² + R<sub>s</sub>² = 1 would allow 34.4 MPa, 20% too much: an unsafe answer.
examples.answer: σ<sub>cr</sub> = 26.58 MPa, τ<sub>cr</sub> = 38.51 MPa; R<sub>c</sub> + R<sub>s</sub>² = 0.72, MS = 0.26; with 12 MPa compression the panel takes up to 28.5 MPa of shear.

examples.question: The square plate of the earlier chapters, 800 mm × 800 mm × 4 mm with E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.30 and simply supported edges, is loaded in pure shear. Find N<sub>xy,cr</sub>, the shear stress at buckling and the total shear force on one edge, and compare with its compressive buckling load.
steps: Edge force: N<sub>xy,cr</sub> × 0.8 m = 47,323 N = 47.3 kN.
Compression alone buckles it at 4π²D/b² = 25.3 kN/m, so the plate takes 2.34 times as much shear flow as compression before it buckles, the ratio 9.35/4.
examples.answer: N<sub>xy,cr</sub> = 59.2 kN/m, τ<sub>cr</sub> = 14.79 MPa, 47.3 kN per edge; 2.34 times the compressive buckling load.

traps: Using the circle R<sub>c</sub>² + R<sub>s</sub>² = 1 for compression with shear. The curve for a long flat panel is R<sub>c</sub> + R<sub>s</sub>² = 1; the circle overestimates the allowable shear.
Using k<sub>c</sub> = 4 for shear. The shear coefficient of a simply supported panel is 5.35 + 4(b/a)², 9.35 for a square.
Taking b as the longer side. In both k<sub>s</sub> and τ<sub>cr</sub>, b is the shorter side of the panel.
Adding stresses in different directions, σ + τ, and comparing with one allowable. Each load is divided by its own critical value first.
Treating τ<sub>cr</sub> as the collapse load of a web. A buckled web carries more shear as a tension field, if its flanges and stiffeners can take it.

quiz.q: Write the interaction equation for a long flat panel under compression and shear, and define the ratios.
quiz.a: R<sub>c</sub> + R<sub>s</sub>² = 1, with R<sub>c</sub> = σ/σ<sub>cr</sub> and R<sub>s</sub> = τ/τ<sub>cr</sub>, each critical stress for that load acting alone.

quiz.q: Why can a plate buckle under shear alone?
quiz.a: Pure shear equals tension on one 45° diagonal and compression on the other. The compressed diagonal behaves like a strut and buckles, wrinkling the plate in inclined waves.

quiz.q: A long panel has σ<sub>cr</sub> = 40 MPa and τ<sub>cr</sub> = 80 MPa. With σ = 24 MPa, find the shear stress at buckling.
Find the margin of safety of a panel with R<sub>c</sub> = 0.5 and R<sub>s</sub> = 0.5.
Explain why the shear ratio appears squared in the interaction equation while the compression ratio does not.
quiz.a: Shear of either sign buckles the panel equally, because reversing it only mirrors the inclined wave; the interaction curve must be symmetric in R<sub>s</sub>, which an even power gives. Compression and tension are not equivalent (tension raises the buckling load), so R<sub>c</sub> enters with its sign, linearly.

quiz.q: A designer stiffens the panel of the first example by halving its width between stringers. What happens to σ<sub>cr</sub>, τ<sub>cr</sub> and the margin, roughly?
quiz.a: Both critical stresses vary as 1/b², so they rise about four times (k<sub>s</sub> also rises a little as b/a grows). R<sub>c</sub> and R<sub>s</sub> fall about four times, R<sub>c</sub> + R<sub>s</sub>² falls well below 1, and the margin rises from 0.26 to about 3.9 (computing it with the new k<sub>s</sub> = 5.46).

beyond: Not for the exam. Interaction curves for real panels with cut-outs, stiffeners and composite lay-ups come from finite element eigenvalue analysis and tests. Curved fuselage panels have their own shear coefficients that grow with curvature. Search for shear buckling coefficient and combined loading interaction curves.
